facts.value: 29173 (Appendix F, Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27) is a 17-page CIPFA-Code strategy paper. Council-specific figures live in five tables (7.1, Schedule 2 Sections 1-4, and the Treasury Management Indicators). Companion paper 30311 (Treasury Management 2025/26 outturn, Audit Committee 9 July 2026) carries the year-end position, deposit list, interest cost and rate range — both papers are read together for the reconciliation and the note.

No LOBOs, no market debt, no bank loans. Forecast reduction of £1,950k per year (Schedule 2 Sec 4) reflects the two annuity loans' amortisation. Outturn actuals for 2025/26 = £2,008,545 reduction (£1,996,561 annuity principal + £11,984 interest accrual).

facts.value: Negative every year: (0.27) actual 2024/25 improving to (0.17) by 2029/30. Net investment income (interest receivable + investment income) exceeds financing costs (interest payable + MRP).

source.title: Appendix F Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Schedule 2 Section 1

summary.text:
A clean, conventional treasury picture at a well-run district council. Our PWLB price book returns 8 loans for East Hampshire totalling £114,443,571 at a weighted 2.3541%, 6 maturity plus 2 annuity — matching the closing balances in Table 1 of the 2025/26 outturn (£38,043,570 annuity + £76,400,000 maturity = £114,443,570) to £1 on principal and to the count and shape of the book. One of the cleanest reconciliations we have run.

The balance-sheet identity ties: CFR closing £155,137k at 31 March 2025 less external PWLB £117,102k less £5,379k of other long-term liabilities = £32,656k of internal borrowing. The paper prints an 'Over/(Under) Borrowing' figure of £39,439k in Schedule 2 Sec 4 which is a different calculation (uses opening rather than closing CFR, does not deduct OLTL) — ties to their own arithmetic but is not the CIPFA-conventional internal borrowing measure. Delta £1.4m, not worth raising.

Forward, the picture is quiet. Approved borrowing requirement is ZERO for every year of the 2025/26-2029/30 capital programme; CFR runs down only through MRP (£155.1m to £143.4m by 31 March 2030). The outturn confirms no new loans in 2025/26 and the earliest maturity is £10m at 2.07% on 21/12/2028 — that is the first refinancing decision, roughly a three-point uplift against the strategy's own 25-year PWLB forecast of 5.0%. £15m at 2.27% follows on 16/06/2029. Beyond 2029 nothing matures until 2033. On today's DMO premature repayment curve the whole book sits below par — indicatively about £17.8m under principal in aggregate — but the council states outright that receipts from asset disposals are ringfenced for investing not for repaying PWLB.

The one real change year-on-year is on the deposit side: investment position rose from £22.29m at 31 March 2025 (strategy Table 7.1) to £60m at 31 March 2026 (outturn §4.2) — a £40m upside on the strategy's forecast, driven by asset disposals ringfenced for treasury per §3.2. Deposit list at year-end is short-duration (longest 9 months, Lloyds at 4.50%) and diversified across SMBC, Qatar National Bank, National Bank of Kuwait, OCBC, National Bank of Canada, Lloyds, Landesbank Hessen-Thueringen. Deposit income £1.666m in-year against £2.718m of PWLB interest cost.

The S151 is Matthew Tiller, Chief Finance Officer — named on the outturn (doc 30311, sign-off block and Contact Officer p.4). Email published: matthew.tiller@easthants.gov.uk. Strategy paper alone does not name him. External treasury adviser is MUFG (formerly Link Group). Draft written and machine-checked; recipient known. Status: ready to send.

officer.body:
Hi Matthew,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy Council approved on 26 February and the 2025/26 outturn Audit Committee took on 9 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your papers are clear and well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A cross-check first, which comes out unusually clean. Our PWLB price book holds 8 loans for East Hampshire totalling £114,443,571 at a weighted 2.3541%, 6 maturity plus 2 annuity. Your outturn Table 1 on page 3 gives £38,043,570 annuity plus £76,400,000 maturity at 31 March 2026 — £114,443,570 on principal, with the £649,059 interest accrual sitting on top for the £115,092,629 total. Same eight loans on both sides, a match to £1 on the closing balance, and the 1.95%-to-2.76% range at paragraph 5.3 is the same range as the individual-loans view in Table 3 of Appendix F. As clean a reconciliation as we get, and it means the rest of this note is being measured off the same book.

The picture that falls out of it is stable. Your Schedule 2 Section 4 in Appendix F has CFR closing at £155.1m at 31 March 2025 running down to £143.4m by 2029/30 as MRP charges through, and the approved borrowing requirement is zero every year of the plan. The outturn confirms no new loans in 2025/26 either. So the book is on a runoff from here — every one of your eight loans sits below par on today's DMO premature repayment curve, indicatively about £17.8m under principal in aggregate. That is context only. The DMO's quote is the only binding one, we don't model MRP or accounting treatment, and your outturn at 3.2 is explicit that the ringfenced disposal receipts are for investing, not for repaying PWLB. Where the book runs to on today's curve is on your loan page at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The first maturity is where the arithmetic gets interesting. £10m of the interest-only book runs off on 21 December 2028 at 2.07% — Appendix F Table 3. Your strategy at paragraph 8.3 has 25-year PWLB at 5.0% forecast, and the outturn at 5.3 puts current rates at 5% plus, so whatever piece of that £10m needs to be replaced would price at roughly a three-point uplift. £15m at 2.27% follows on 16 June 2029 in the same shape. Beyond 2029 nothing matures until 2033. The question the paper doesn't answer either way is how much of the 2028-29 maturity is actually being replaced given CFR is still running down through the same window — and the liability benchmark is the tool the incoming CIPFA Code refresh will put more centrally in strategy papers to help frame that decision, so worth having a live view of yours by the time the 2027/28 strategy is drafted.

The other change worth naming is the deposit side. Your investment position rose from £22.29m at 31 March 2025 (strategy Table 7.1) to £60m at 31 March 2026 (outturn 4.2) — a £40m upside on the strategy's own forecast of c£20m, driven by asset disposals ringfenced for treasury per outturn 3.2. £1.67m of deposit income in the year against £2.72m of PWLB interest cost, so the treasury book is now net cash-cost of just over £1m before the wider investment-income lines. Your March list is short-duration and diversified — SMBC (twice), Qatar National Bank, National Bank of Kuwait, OCBC, National Bank of Canada, Lloyds and Landesbank Hessen-Thueringen. A live view of who else in the sector is placing similar duration and where is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four look most relevant. Liability Benchmark: the essentials sits right against the CIPFA Prudential and Treasury Code refresh that's coming. Strategic PWLB borrowing is written for exactly the December 2028 decision. Interest rate risk speaks to the £60m short-duration deposit book. Treasury management for councillors is written for Audit Committee members. All 116 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
